newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seems set for victory as America votes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seems set for victory as America votes.

text.p: Americans headed for the polls on Tuesday with all signs pointing to a triumph for President Bill Clinton and the end of the trail for old soldier Bob Dole.

But the opinion surveys that unanimously forecast re-election for Democrat Clinton also suggest that grudging voters -- happy enough economically but uninspired by Clinton personally -- might check him with another Republican Congress or even deny him the majority popular support he covets.

Late polls said the Republicans seemed likely to retain control of the 100-member Senate. But the 435-seat House of Representatives was rated too close to call and Clinton's personal support hovered around the 50 percent mark in surveys where many seemed to look upon him the lesser of two evils.

Clinton, 50, hoping to become the first Democrat re-elected U.S. president since 1944, would have to sweat out the verdict until Tuesday night along with Dole, 73, an ex-Kansas senator and Second World War infantryman pursuing "one last mission."
Waiting with them was Ross Perot, the Texas billionaire who took nearly one vote in five in a 1992 presidential bid but seemed a far weaker force this time around.
Most polls close between 7 p.m. EDT (0001 Wednesday) in some Eastern states and 11 p.m. EDT (0400 GMT) in California.
The White House result should be known by mid-evening but control of Congress may not be clear until Wednesday, if then.

At stake besides the White House and Congress were 11 of 50 state governorships, many local offices and ballot issues ranging from whether Californians wish to use marijuana as medicine to whether Floridians will safeguard the Everglades.

The vote concluded another long, exhausting and costly U.S. election cycle that began as a high-toned promise of leadership into the 21st Century and ended as a brawl dominated by attacks on Clinton's character and the alleged influence of foreign cash in his campaign and his government.
These blows caused a late sag in his big polling leads and set pulses to racing among Dole partisans -- although if they fazed the confident Clinton, he never let on.

Dole, his voice reduced to a fatigued croak, barnstormed gamely through a 96-hour, 17-state campaign finale through the last night and into Election Day, dragging a punchy entourage through airports, meeting halls, diners and ice cream parlours.

"I may not keep my voice but I will keep my word," he told one crowd in Phoenix in a dig at Clinton. "I will not violate the public trust when I'm president of the United States. I've never known such arrogance in the White House."

His last road stop was to be in Independence, Missouri, the home of the late President Harry Truman, for a bow to Dole's dream of duplicating Truman's historic upset of Republican Thomas Dewey in the 1948 presidential election.
But every scrap of polling evidence suggested a Dole victory would dwarf even that political shocker -- and there were signs he and his top strategists knew it.

A New Yorker magazine article out on Monday quoted Dole campaign manager Scott Reed as saying in an interview last week: "I have told him -- I tell him every morning -- I say, 'It looks like we may not win.' And he says, 'you're right.'"

Election eve surveys gave Clinton leads ranging from about seven points in a Reuters poll to 18 in a CBS/New York Times survey, with most in between. Clinton's support was in the 47-53 percent range, with Dole at or below 40 percent and Perot at eight or nine points.

Clinton's lead has wavered little all year and the reason was clear: he can point to a country that is prosperous, at peace and without scarring social turmoil. Unemployment is at a seven-year low of 5.2 percent, inflation is only about 3 percent, stock market indices are sky-high, the federal deficit is barely over one-third what it was when he took office and crime rates are the lowest in a decade.
Against all that, Dole's main promises -- lower taxes and a higher moral tone in the White House -- have not sold.
Poll after poll including a new ABC survey show voters prefer Clinton's competence and understanding of their problems to Dole's honesty and intergrity, by huge margins.

But in so doing they indicate they do not think highly of Clinton personally. Fifty-two percent in the ABC poll said "they did not regard him as honest and trustworthy," a finding that duplicates similar condemnations in many other surveys.
Voting analysts said that attitude could aggravate the U.S. tendency toward low voter participation, perhaps depress this one near the record low 50 percent turnout in 1988.

Low turnouts usually hurt Democrats more than Republicans, and could in this case undercut the Democratic drive to regain control of the House and to give Clinton -- elected with only 43 percent support 1992 -- the majority mandate he craves.

Under the indirect U.S. system, however, presidential elections are really 50 separate state contests with the winner in each getting all of that state's electoral votes. Clinton's electoral vote lead looked unassailable.
